title: On Theosis
subtitle: The highest and ultimate purpose for which we were created.
summary: Theosis, deification by grace, is the goal of the Christian life. We participate in the uncreated energies of God without participating in his essence, and so become by grace what God is by nature.

essay.text: It is daring to speak of theosis without first having tasted it. We dare what is beyond our power because we trust in the mercy of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. We speak so that we do not hide from our brothers the highest and ultimate purpose of our life, the purpose for which we were created. We speak so that it becomes clear that the only truly Orthodox form of pastoral guidance is that which is intended to lead to theosis, and which is not, as in Western Christianity, aimed at a moral perfection that does not depend on God's grace.

We speak so that all may desire what is best and struggle for the highest. This alone is able to quench the depth of the soul's thirst for the Absolute, the Triune God. We speak so that we may overflow with gratitude towards our Maker and Creator for his great gift, theosis by grace; so that we may realise the irreplaceability of the Holy Church as the only community of theosis on earth; so that our souls may be consoled, for however poisoned and darkened by sin they have been, they yearn for the light of Christ's face.

Theosis is a gift of God's grace, but it still requires effort on our part. It does not mean we become divine by nature. If we participated in God's essence the distinction between God and man would be abolished, and the Church teaches no such thing. What it means is that we participate in God's uncreated energies, described in Scripture by many terms: glory, life, love, virtue, power.

We are to become like God by his grace, and so to be truly his adopted children, but never to become God by nature. That is the reason the Christian life has so many "commandments". The Psalmist understood this when he wrote Psalm 119. There we see a deep love for God's commandments, statutes, judgments, and laws, all of which are synonyms for the way of life God has given. The Psalmist pursues all of these with his whole heart, even saying that they enlarge his heart (v. 32).

The Fathers' rule is exact: God became man so that man might become god. This was not invented by Athanasius or Irenaeus. It is the apostolic confession applied to the Incarnation. Because the Word assumed our nature without sin, our nature is divinized in him without being changed into the divine nature. The hypostatic union in Christ is the ground of every union by grace in us.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: The Holy Spirit reproaches men because they were made like God, free from suffering and death, provided that they kept his commandments, and were deemed deserving of the name of his sons; and yet, becoming like Adam and Eve, they work out death for themselves. Let the interpretation of the Psalm be held just as you wish, yet thereby it is demonstrated that all men are deemed worthy of becoming gods, and of having power to become sons of the Highest.
florilegium.gloss: The earliest Greek apologist puts the doctrine plainly: men are made worthy of becoming gods by grace.

florilegium.author: St Irenaeus of Lyons
florilegium.reference: Book III, Preface and Book V
florilegium.text: He speaks undoubtedly these words to those who have not received the gift of adoption, but who despise the incarnation of the pure generation of the Word of God, defraud human nature of promotion into God, and prove themselves ungrateful to the Word of God who became flesh for them. For it was for this end that the Word of God was made man, and he who was the Son of God became the Son of man, that man, having been taken into the Word and receiving the adoption, might become the Son of God.
florilegium.gloss: Irenaeus' rule of exchange, the ground of every later patristic statement on theosis.

florilegium.author: St Theophilus of Antioch
florilegium.text: Man was neither made by nature mortal nor immortal, but, as we have said above, capable of both: so that if he should incline to the things of immortality, keeping the commandment of God, he should receive as reward from him immortality, and should become God; but if, on the other hand, he should turn to the things of death, disobeying God, he should himself be the cause of death to himself.
florilegium.gloss: The pre-Nicene witness that the destiny of man is to become god.

florilegium.author: St Maximus the Confessor
florilegium.text: A sure warrant for looking forward with hope to the deification of human nature is provided by the Incarnation of God, which makes man God to the same degree as God himself became man. Let us become the image of the one whole God, bearing nothing earthly in ourselves, so that we may consort with God and become gods, receiving from God our existence as gods. For it is clear that he who became man without sin will divinize human nature without changing it into the divine nature, and will raise it up for his own sake to the same degree as he lowered himself for man's sake. This is what Saint Paul teaches mystically when he says, 'that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace' (Ephesians 2:7).
florilegium.gloss: Maximus, the doctor of theosis: the Incarnation is the warrant for our deification.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
florilegium.text: He became man that we might be made god; and he manifested himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and he endured the insolence of men, that we might inherit immortality.
florilegium.gloss: The classical formulation of the rule of exchange.
